How to check resale value in Europe: apps and methods compared

There is no single perfect source for second-hand prices. Each method below answers a slightly different question. Here is what each one is good at, where it falls short, and when to use it.

Updated 2026-10-12 · by FlipLens

FlipLens

FlipLens identifies the exact model from a photo, barcode or typed name, reads comparable active eBay listings in five EU countries or on eBay.co.uk, removes other variants, bundles and broken items, adjusts for condition and returns a resale range, your profit after fees and shipping and the most you should pay. Good for: fast buying decisions at flea markets and on classifieds, when you do not want to research every item by hand. Limits: it works from asking prices, not confirmed sale prices; it covers consumer electronics, gaming, cameras and power tools, not fashion; if there are too few comparable listings it says so instead of estimating. See how it works.

eBay search with the "Sold items" filter

On eBay you can filter a search to show items that actually sold. Better than FlipLens at: showing real final prices rather than asking prices. Drawbacks: you check one eBay site at a time, you have to read through the results yourself to remove other generations, bundles and broken items, and you still need to subtract fees and shipping to know your profit. Worth doing for expensive items before you commit.

Searching Vinted or Kleinanzeigen

Searching the marketplace you plan to sell on shows the competition you will face. Good for: local pricing and items that sell mainly through classifieds. Drawbacks: you only see asking prices, and listings that sit unsold for weeks pull the picture up. FlipLens links to these searches from every result so you can compare in a tap.

Google Lens to identify an unknown item

When you do not know what an item is, an image search can find the name or model. Good for: unusual items, vintage pieces and anything without a readable label. Drawbacks: it identifies, it does not price; you still need to search marketplaces and judge condition and variants yourself.

Trade-in and buyback offers

Some shops and websites make an instant offer to buy your used phone, console or camera. Good for: selling quickly with no effort. Drawbacks: the offer is what the buyer is willing to pay to resell it themselves, so it is usually well below what you could get selling privately. It is a floor, not a resale value.

When to use which

  • Standing at a stall, seconds to decide: FlipLens.
  • An expensive item before you buy: FlipLens first, then the eBay sold filter to confirm.
  • Pricing your own listing: look at what is for sale on your marketplace right now.
  • No idea what the item is: Google Lens first.
  • You just want it gone: a trade-in offer, knowing it is the lowest number.

Questions

What is the most accurate way to find resale value?

Recent sold prices for the exact model in the same condition, adjusted for fees and shipping. eBay's sold filter shows them for one country at a time; FlipLens gives a fast estimate from active listings across five EU countries or on eBay.co.uk.

Why are trade-in offers so low?

The buyer has to resell the item and make a profit, so the offer is below the private resale price.

Is there a free way to check resale value?

Yes. Marketplace searches and the eBay sold filter are free, and FlipLens includes 10 free checks a month.
